title: Not to worry
description: There is no need for concern.
details:
Example: Not to worry; we can catch the next bus.

Usage: Conversational British reassurance.

title: A bit of a faff
description: Something inconvenient and fiddly to do.
details:
Example: Setting up the printer was a bit of a faff.

Usage: Informal British expression; a minor hassle.

title: I can’t be bothered
description: I do not want to make the effort.
details:
Example: I can’t be bothered to cook tonight.

Usage: Informal; can sound dismissive about duties.

title: It’s not the end of the world
description: The problem is manageable.
details:
Example: We lost a point; it’s not the end of the world.

Usage: Conversational; reassure without minimising serious distress.

title: That’s a bit steep
description: That price seems too high.
details:
Example: Ten pounds for a sandwich? That’s a bit steep.

Usage: Informal British usage; comment on price.

title: Cheap and cheerful
description: Inexpensive but pleasant and adequate.
details:
Example: We found a cheap and cheerful café.

Usage: Informal British expression; mildly approving.

title: It’s swings and roundabouts
description: The gains and losses roughly balance.
details:
Example: The commute is longer but cheaper; it’s swings and roundabouts.

Usage: Informal British expression; offsetting advantages.

title: Horses for courses
description: Different choices suit different situations or people.
details:
Example: You like big cities; I prefer villages. Horses for courses.

Usage: Informal British expression; accept different preferences.

title: Don’t get your hopes up
description: Do not expect success too confidently.
details:
Example: Ask about tickets, but don’t get your hopes up.

Usage: Conversational; manage expectations.

title: At a loose end
description: Without anything particular to do.
details:
Example: I’m at a loose end this afternoon.

Usage: Informal British usage; free and perhaps bored.

title: Under the weather
description: Feeling slightly unwell.
details:
Example: I’m a bit under the weather today.

Usage: Conversational; usually a minor illness.

title: A storm in a teacup
description: Excessive fuss over a minor issue.
details:
Example: The row about the chairs was a storm in a teacup.

Usage: British expression; dismisses an argument as exaggerated.

title: Put a spanner in the works
description: Cause a plan to go wrong.
details:
Example: The strike put a spanner in the works.

Usage: Informal British expression; disrupt arrangements.

title: Take it with a pinch of salt
description: Treat the claim with some scepticism.
details:
Example: Take his stories with a pinch of salt.

Usage: Conversational British wording; question reliability.

title: Not my finest hour
description: A moment when I performed badly.
details:
Example: Forgetting her name was not my finest hour.

Usage: Conversational; understated or humorous self-criticism.

title: I’m chuffed to bits
description: I am very pleased and proud.
details:
Example: I’m chuffed to bits with my results.

Usage: Informal British expression; enthusiastic satisfaction.

title: I’m absolutely shattered
description: I am extremely tired.
details:
Example: After that shift, I’m absolutely shattered.

Usage: Informal British usage; exhaustion.

title: It’s a bit of a grey area
description: The rules or boundaries are unclear.
details:
Example: Working during leave is a bit of a grey area.

Usage: Neutral; unclear interpretation, not merely unknown facts.

title: You’ve hit the nail on the head
description: You have identified the issue exactly.
details:
Example: That’s the problem; you’ve hit the nail on the head.

Usage: Conversational; endorse a precise observation.

title: Let’s not beat about the bush
description: Let’s discuss the main issue directly.
details:
Example: Let’s not beat about the bush: we need help.

Usage: Conversational British wording; ask for directness.
